# Volume 5 — CHAPTER VII. A FISHY EPISODE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Tessa Carrow made her way with pride, and maybe a slight touch of primness, along the primary “street” of the Glen before ascending the manse hill, cautiously bearing a tiny basket filled with early strawberries that Tabitha had nurtured into mouth-watering perfection inside a sunlit corner of Hollowmere. Instructions had been given to Tessa by Tabitha that she must hand over the basket to no one other than Aunt Martha or Mr. Ashdown, and Tessa, feeling immense pride in being given this task, was determined to follow those directions precisely.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0000 }

Tabitha had clad her finely in a pale, stiffened, and worked frock, accompanied by a blue sash and slippers covered in beads. Her lengthy reddish ringlets were smooth and shaped, and Tabitha had permitted her to wear her finest hat, as a gesture of respect toward the manse. It was a rather intricate creation, in which the preference of Tabitha had exerted greater influence than that of Nell, and the little spirit of Tessa exulted in its magnificence of silk, lace, and blossoms. She felt extremely mindful of her hat, and I fear she marched proudly up the manse hill. That proud march, or the hat, or the two together, annoyed Mary Stubbs, who was swinging upon the gate of the lawn. Furthermore, the mood of Mary was rather agitated at that moment. Aunt Martha had denied her permission to scrape the potatoes and had commanded her to leave the kitchen.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0001 }

“Yah! You’ll carry the potatoes to the table with pieces of skin hanging off them and only half cooked as usual! My, but going to your funeral will be wonderful,” Mary shrieked. Leaving the kitchen, she slammed the door with such force that even Aunt Martha heard the sound, while Mr. Ashdown felt the tremor in his study, vaguely suspecting a minor earthquake had occurred. After that, he resumed writing his sermon.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0002 }

Mary glided away from the gate to face the immaculate young woman from Hollowmere.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0003 }

“What’s in that basket?” she asked forcefully, attempting to grab it from me.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0004 }

Tessa put up a struggle, lisping, “Mithter Ashdown is supposed to have it.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0005 }

“Hand it over to me so that I can hand it over to him,” Mary stated.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0006 }

“No. Thuthan told me that Mithter Mer’dith or Aunt Martha were the only ones I should hand it to,” Tessa maintained.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0007 }

Mary eyed her sourly.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0008 }

“You imagine you are special, do you not, completely attired like a plaything! Observe me. My clothing is entirely tattered and I am indifferent! I would prefer being in tatters to being a miniature doll. Return to your home and instruct them to place you inside a display cabinet. Observe me—observe me—observe me!”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0009 }

Mary performed a frantic dance encircling the appalled and confused Tessa, tossing her tattered skirt and shouting “Look at me—look at me” to the point that unfortunate Tessa became lightheaded. However, when Tessa attempted to sidestep in the direction of the gate, Mary sprang upon her once more.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0010 }

“Hand that basket over to me,” she demanded, making a face. Mary had perfected the skill of “making faces.” She was able to distort her features into an exceedingly bizarre and uncanny expression, from which her unusual, glowing, pale eyes shone to eerie effect.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0011 }

“I won’t,” Tessa gasped, terrified yet resolute. “You let me go, Mary Vanth.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0012 }

Mary released her hold for a moment and surveyed her surroundings. Right within the entrance stood a modest “flake,” where six sizable codfish were in the process of drying. A member of Mr. Ashdown’s congregation had given them to him on a certain day, maybe instead of the contribution he was expected to contribute toward the salary but failed to. Mr. Ashdown had expressed his gratitude to the man and subsequently completely wiped the fish from his mind, and they would have quickly rotted if the untiring Mary had not readied them for the drying process and constructed the “flake” with her own hands to dry them on.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0013 }

An evil idea struck Mary. Rushing over to the “flake,” she grabbed the biggest fish on it—an enormous, flat specimen that was almost the size of her own body. Shouting loudly, she charged at the frightened Tessa while waving her strange weapon. Tessa lost her nerve. Being beaten with a dried codfish was an unprecedented ordeal that Tessa was unable to confront. Screaming, she let go of her basket and ran away. The lovely berries, which Tabitha had picked with such care for the minister, spilled in a pink stream across the dusty road, getting crushed beneath the running feet of both the chaser and the chased. Mary was no longer thinking about the basket or what it held. Her sole focus was the joy of scaring Tessa Carrow as she had never been scared before. She intended to show her not to act superior just because she wore fancy garments.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0014 }

Tessa hurried rapidly down the slope and down the road. Fear gave speed to her steps, allowing her to stay barely in front of Mary, who was slowed down a bit by her laughing, although she possessed sufficient wind to let out periodically terrifying yells while she hurried, waving her codfish around. Along the Glen street they rushed, as all the people rushed to their windows and gates so they could watch them. Mary sensed that she was causing a huge stir, which gave her pleasure. Tessa, unable to see due to her fright and deprived of air, believed she was incapable of continuing to run. Within a moment that dreadful girl was going to reach her with the codfish. Just then the unfortunate small child tripped and collapsed inside the puddle of mud located where the street ended, right when Miss Winifred emerged from Carter Flagg’s shop.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0015 }

Miss Winifred understood everything immediately. Mary did as well. Halting abruptly in her wild dash, Mary spun about prior to any words from Miss Winifred, fleeing upward with the same speed she had used coming down. Although Miss Winifred’s mouth set in a threatening line, she recognized the futility of trying to pursue her. Consequently, she lifted the miserable, crying, untidy Tessa in her arms and brought her back to the house. Tessa was devastated. Not only were her hat, dress, and slippers destroyed, but a severe blow had also been dealt to her six-year-old pride.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0016 }

As her face grew pale from anger, Tabitha listened to the tale recounted by Miss Winifred regarding what Mary Stubbs had done.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0017 }

“Oh, the hussy—oh, the littly hussy!” she declared, while taking Tessa off to be cleansed and consoled.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0018 }

“Nell dearie, this thing has gone far enough,” Miss Winifred stated resolutely. “We must do something. Who is the creature staying at the manse, and from where does she come?”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0019 }

“It was my understanding that she was a young girl from over-harbour visiting the manse,” replied Nell, seeing how funny the codfish pursuit had been while privately believing that Tessa possessed too much vanity and required a few lessons.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0020 }

“I am acquainted with every family from across the harbour who attends our church, and that little devil isn't part of any of them,” Miss Winifred countered. “She is practically dressed in rags, and on the occasions she attends church, she puts on Grace Ashdown’s cast-off garments. A mystery exists here, and I intend to get to the bottom of it, because it appears no one else has any intention of doing so. It is my belief that she was behind their antics in Warren Mead’s spruce bush recently. Have you heard about them scaring his mother so badly she had a fit?”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0021 }

“No. I was aware that Hugh was summoned to her presence, yet the nature of the issue remained unknown to me.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0022 }

“Well, you are aware that her heart is weak. And last week, on a particular day when she was by herself on the veranda, the most terrible screams of ‘murder’ and ‘help’ reached her from the bush—truly horrific noises, Nell dearie. Right away, her heart failed. Warren listened to them too from the barn, going directly to the bush to see what was happening, where he discovered every one of the manse children perched on a downed tree, shouting ‘murder’ as loudly as they could. They explained to him that it was merely a game and they assumed nobody would catch the sound. They were simply pretending to be an Indian ambush. Returning to the house, Warren discovered his unfortunate mother out cold on the veranda.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0023 }

Tabitha, who was back, gave a scornful sniff.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0024 }

“It is my belief that she was nowhere near losing consciousness, Mrs. Ambrose Kerr, and you can rely on that. Amelia Warren’s bad heart has been brought to my attention for a period of forty years. It was already a problem when her age was twenty. Making a spectacle and calling the physician brings her pleasure, and she will use any pretext.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0025 }

“Hugh did not consider her illness particularly severe, in my opinion,” Nell stated.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0026 }

“Ah, that might indeed be true,” Miss Winifred remarked. “However, the situation has generated an immense amount of gossip, and the fact that the Meads are Methodists renders it even more terrible. What will happen to those kids? At times, the thought of them keeps me awake during the night, my dear Nell. I genuinely doubt whether they even receive sufficient food, since their father is so absorbed in his reveries that he rarely recalls his own appetite, and that slothful elderly woman fails to cook proper meals. They are simply roaming without restraint, and with the school term ending, their behavior will become even more untamed.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0027 }

“Indeed, they enjoy happy moments,” Nell remarked, chuckling as she remembered several events from Fern Hollow that she had heard about. “Furthermore, each one of them is courageous, open, faithful, and honest.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0028 }

“What you say is correct, my dear Nell, and considering every bit of the discord in the congregation that was caused by the previous minister’s two gossiping, dishonest children, I am disposed to forgive many things about the Ashdowns.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0029 }

“All things considered, Mrs. Dr. dear, those kids are quite lovely,” Tabitha remarked. “I shall grant that they possess an abundance of original sin, yet perhaps that is for the best, since without it they could be ruined by being too sweet. I must insist, however, that playing inside a cemetery is simply unsuitable for them.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0030 }

“However, their games are actually rather subdued in that spot,” Nell offered in defense. “Unlike in other places, they refrain from racing about and shouting. Occasionally, such shrieks float up to this place from Fern Hollow! Even so, I imagine my own little ones contribute bravely to the racket. According to Kit, they engaged in a mock fight there yesterday evening and were forced to ‘roar’ on their own, given their lack of cannons for making noise. Kit is currently going through that phase when every boy yearns to become a soldier.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0031 }

“Thank goodness, he will definitely not become a soldier,” Miss Winifred stated. “Our boys going off to that conflict in South Africa was something I never supported. However, that is finished, and another event like it is improbable. The world seems to be gaining sense, in my view. Regarding the Ashdowns, my opinion has often been expressed and I repeat it now: everything would be fine if a wife were present for Mr. Ashdown.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0032 }

“I have been informed that he visited the Kirks on two occasions during the previous week,” Tabitha remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0033 }

“Well,” Miss Winifred uttered reflectively, “usually, I am against a clergyman finding a wife among his flock. Most times, it ruins him. However, it wouldn't cause any trouble here, because Elizabeth Kirk is beloved by all, and no one else desires the task of becoming a stepmother to those children. The Hill sisters shrink from it, too. They have not been seen setting snares for Mr. Ashdown. Should he merely realize it, Elizabeth would prove a fine spouse to him. Yet the issue remains that she is genuinely plain, and, my dear Nell, Mr. Ashdown, despite his dreaminess, appreciates an attractive female, just as men do. Trust me, he is not quite so heavenly minded regarding that matter.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0034 }

“Elizabeth Kirk is an extremely pleasant individual, but it is indeed rumored that individuals have almost perished from the cold in her mother’s guest bed previously, Mrs. Dr. dear,” Tabitha stated ominously. “If I believed I possessed any standing to voice an idea regarding so serious a subject as a clergyman’s wedding I would state that I believe Sarah, Elizabeth’s cousin across the harbor, would prove a superior spouse to Mr. Ashdown.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0035 }

“Indeed, Sarah Kirk belongs to the Methodists,” stated Miss Winifred, in a manner quite like Tabitha had proposed a Hottentot to be the wife at the manse.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0036 }

“Were she to wed Mr. Ashdown, she would probably become a Presbyterian,” Tabitha snapped back.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0037 }

Miss Winifred gave a shake of her head. It was clear that for her, being a Methodist once meant remaining a Methodist forever.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0038 }

“Sarah Kirk cannot be considered at all,” she asserted with certainty. “Emmeline Drew is equally impossible—even if the entire Drew family is attempting to bring about the marriage. They are quite literally flinging poor Emmeline in his direction, while he remains completely unaware of what they are doing.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0039 }

“I have to concede that Emmeline Drew lacks any drive,” Tabitha remarked. “Mrs. Dr. dear, she belongs to that class of women who would place a hot-water bottle inside your bed during a sweltering dog-night, and subsequently feel offended when you failed to show gratitude. Furthermore, her mother managed a home quite poorly. Were you ever told the tale regarding her dishcloth? On a certain day, she misplaced her dishcloth. However, she discovered it on the following day. Indeed, Mrs. Dr. dear, it was located by her right in the dinner-table goose, blended into the stuffing. Is it your opinion that a minister’s mother-in-law ought to be a woman of that sort? It is not mine. Nevertheless, fixing little Kit’s trousers would surely be a superior use of my time than spreading rumors regarding those who live near me. They were ripped by him in a truly disgraceful manner yesterday evening in Fern Hollow.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0040 }

“Where is Edmund?” Nell asked.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0041 }

“I am afraid he is planning some mischief, Mrs. Dr. dear. Up in the attic, he is putting words into an exercise book. Furthermore, the teacher informs me that his arithmetic performance was not up to standard this term. The cause of this is all too clear to me. Instead of practicing his sums, he spent his time composing foolish verses. Mrs. Dr. dear, I fear the boy will end up as a poet.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0042 }

“At present, Tabitha, he has become a poet.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0043 }

“Indeed, your composure is remarkable, dear Mrs. Dr. Assuming one possesses the fortitude, I imagine that is the finest approach. A relative of mine, an uncle, started out as a poet and ultimately became a vagrant. My family felt immense embarrassment on his account.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0044 }

“It appears you hold a rather low opinion of poets, Tabitha,” Nell said with a laugh.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0045 }

“Who does that, Mrs. Dr. dear?” Tabitha inquired, truly amazed.
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0046 }

“How about Shakespeare and Milton? As well as the poets in the Bible?”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0047 }

“It is said to me that Milton failed to live peaceably with his wife, and Shakespeare was merely decent on occasion. Regarding the Bible, naturally matters were otherwise during those holy times—even if I have always held a low view of King David, regardless of what anyone says. Writing poetry has never brought about any benefit in my experience, and I trust and petition that that precious boy will leave the inclination behind. Should he fail to do so—it remains for us to observe what a cod-liver oil emulsion can accomplish.”
{: #nw-v05-c07-p0048 }
